questions.question_text: Gender identity is defined as which of the following?

options.text: An individual's perception and self-awareness of being male or female.
The culturally defined behavior that an individual engages in that identifies him or her to others as being male or female.
An individual's erotic attraction to men, women, or both.
An individual's sexual differentiation based on genetics and development in utero.
The biologically determined behavior that an individual engages in that identifies him or her to others as being male or female.

correct_answer.text: An individual's perception and self-awareness of being male or female.

correct_answers.text: An individual's perception and self-awareness of being male or female.

questions.explanation: Gender and sexuality are core aspects of the human experience. Consequently, medical students and students of psychiatry should be informed and conversant about such issues as normative sexual development, gender roles, gender identity, and sexual orientation. Given the complexity of this area, it is important to start with several definitions. Gender identity is an individual’s perception and self-awareness of being male or female. Gender role is the behavior (usually culturally defined) in which an individual engages that identifies him or her to others as being male or female. Sexual orientation “refers to erotic attraction to males, females, or both” (American Psychiatric Association 2000, p. 535).

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorder categories is often associated with gender dysphoria in childhood?

options.text: Bipolar and related disorders.
Disruptive behavior disorders.
Depressive disorders.
Anxiety disorders.
Dissociative disorders.

questions.explanation: Anxiety disorders are often associated with gender identity disorder (called gender dysphoria in DSM-5) in childhood (Coates and Person 1985; Zucker et al. 1996). Wallien et al. (2007a) examined psychiatric comorbidity in a group of 120 Dutch children referred to a gender identity clinic and 47 Dutch children referred to an attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) clinic. Fifty-two percent of children with GID had one or more other diagnoses (such as mood disorders or disruptive behavior disorders), whereas those in the ADHD comparison group were more likely to be diagnosed with an internalizing or externalizing disorder. Additionally, 31% of individuals in the GID group were diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. A study by Wallien et al. (2007b) utilized physiological measures and found that children with GID had more indicators of anxiety than did matched controls. Although this increased anxiety is well documented, some researchers have suggested that it may be adaptive (VanderLaan et al. 2010).

questions.question_text: Which of the following does not represent a popular school of thought with respect to the treatment of prepubertal children with gender dysphoria?

options.text: Fully accommodating the gender identity with which the child identifies and not viewing him or her as disordered.
Focusing on the desires of the parents and accepting that gender dysphoria itself may be a treatment target.
Focusing on the concomitant emotional, behavioral, and family problems that may or may not have an impact on the child's gender dysphoria, rather than on the disorder itself.
Carrying out a comprehensive assessment of the child utilizing validated assessment instruments for gender dysphoria and for co-occurring problems.
Accompanying hormonal treatments with psychotherapy.

questions.explanation: Although physical interventions are not recommended for children with gender dysphoria, they are increasingly considered appropriate as part of the treatment for the adolescent who has persisted with a presentation of gender dysphoria (de Vries et al. 2011; Hembree et al. 2009). Regarding treatment of children, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Task Force on Treatment of Gender Identity Disorder (Byne et al. 2012) noted the absence of randomized controlled outcome studies of children with gender identity disorder and children who are gender variant. The authors of the report stated, “the overarching goal of psychotherapeutic treatment for childhood GID is to optimize the psychological adjustment and well-being of the child” (p. 763). In general, there appear to be several different schools of thought in the approach to the treatment of gender dysphoria in children. Four schools of thought are described in options A through D. For an illustration of option A, see the mission statement of the TransKids Purple Rainbow Foundation (2011). Zucker et al. (2012) outlined an approach similar to that described in option B. Option C is based on the approach described by de Vries and Cohen-Kettenis (2012). The APA Task Force (Byne et al. 2012) has recommended option D.

questions.question_text: Which of the following profiles does not exemplify a child with gender dysphoria?

options.text: A boy who has a preference for simulating female attire.
A girl who stands to urinate.
A boy who expresses the wish to have a vagina.
A girl who engages in sexual experimentation with another girl.
A girl who refuses to play with children of her own sex.

correct_answer.text: A girl who engages in sexual experimentation with another girl.

correct_answers.text: A girl who engages in sexual experimentation with another girl.

questions.explanation: Sexual excitement and experimentation are not addressed by the diagnosis of gender dysphoria. Children with gender dysphoria express a desire to become a member of the opposite gender or some alternative gender different from their assigned gender. Boys may wish to have a vagina and may have a preference for simulating female attire. Girls may wish to have a penis and may simulate a penis with various objects or stand to urinate and may demonstrate a preference for wearing only typical masculine clothing and a strong resistance to wearing typical female clothing. The child also may prefer playmates of the opposite sex, even after most children at the same developmental level have demonstrated a primary preference for playmates of the same sex. This can also extend to preferences for toys, games, or activities of the other gender, as well as a strong rejection of the activities and games typical of their assigned gender. In addition to a strong desire for sex characteristics of their experienced gender, children may also express a strong dislike of their current sexual anatomy. In evaluating a child, it is important not to look solely at behavior; the child must also have a disturbance in sexual/gender identity. As in the evaluation of adults, the clinician should evaluate the child for other psychiatric disorders that are concomitant due to the gender dysphoria (internalizing or externalizing due to social or familial factors).

questions.question_text: The 'watchful waiting' approach to gender dysphoria in children refers to which of the following?

options.text: Deferring treatment until the child declares his or her sexual orientation.
Deferring treatment until the child undergoes puberty.
Treatment whose primary goal is for the child and family to function optimally while waiting to see if the child's gender dysphoria continues into adolescence.
Treatment whose primary goal is to contain symptoms until they make it difficult for the child to function at home or at school.
Deferring treatment until the child asks to be treated.

correct_answer.text: Treatment whose primary goal is for the child and family to function optimally while waiting to see if the child's gender dysphoria continues into adolescence.

correct_answers.text: Treatment whose primary goal is for the child and family to function optimally while waiting to see if the child's gender dysphoria continues into adolescence.

questions.explanation: The “watchful waiting” approach described by de Vries and Cohen-Kettenis (2012) “does not directly target the gender dysphoria itself...[but rather] focuses on its concomitant emotional and behavioral and family problems that may or may not have an impact on the child’s gender dysphoria” (p. 307). The treatment follows a family and parent assessment, as well as an extensive psychodiagnostic assessment of the child. The primary goal of the treatment is for the child and family to function optimally while waiting to see whether the child’s gender dysphoria will continue into adolescence and adulthood. This approach is useful because a majority of children with gender dysphoria will not continue to have gender dysphoria as adults or even adolescents.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about adolescents with gender dysphoria is true?

options.text: Gender dysphoria rarely persists into adulthood.
Adolescent patients generally do not require endocrinological screening unless there is suspicion of a hormonal disorder.
Early surgical intervention is recommended because of better outcomes in terms of healing and scarring.
If the behavior has persisted from childhood into adolescence, it is likely to persist into adulthood.
Adolescent patients do not require a psychiatric examination unless a specific psychiatric problem is suspected.

correct_answer.text: If the behavior has persisted from childhood into adolescence, it is likely to persist into adulthood.

correct_answers.text: If the behavior has persisted from childhood into adolescence, it is likely to persist into adulthood.

questions.explanation: In working with adolescents with gender dysphoria (called gender identity disorder [GID] in DSM-IV), clinicians should bear in mind that if the behavior has persisted from childhood into adolescence, it is likely to persist into adulthood as well; however, they should also recall that the majority of childhood gender dysphoria does not persist into adolescence (Zucker et al. 2012). de Vries recommend a thorough assessment, including a thorough psychiatric examination and a screening by an endocrinologist. There is no empirically or even standardized method for determining which of these adolescents will go on to be diagnosed with gender dysphoria as adults, or go on to have sexual reassignment surgery as adults. Ultimately, any decisions need to be made by the clinician, caregivers, and adolescent with informed consent. Interventions may include individual and family therapy. Adolescents also need to learn coping skills to deal with any harassment or ostracism they may experience. In the Standards of Care for the Health of Transsexual, Transgender, and Gender Nonconforming People, the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (2012) indicates that adolescents may be eligible for fully and partially reversible physical interventions. Although physical interventions are not recommended for children with gender dysphoria, they are increasingly considered appropriate as part of the treatment for the adolescent who has persisted with a presentation of gender dysphoria (de Vries et al. 2011; Hembree et al. 2009).

questions.question_text: Under which of the following conditions should physical interventions be undertaken in adolescents with gender dysphoria?

options.text: After extensive exploration of psychological, family, and social issues.
Starting with partially reversible interventions, such as androgen or estrogen therapy.
Never.
Only after the adolescent has failed to respond to behavioral approaches.
After the adolescent has lived continuously in the gender role congruent with his or her gender identity for at least 6 weeks.

correct_answer.text: After extensive exploration of psychological, family, and social issues.

correct_answers.text: After extensive exploration of psychological, family, and social issues.

questions.explanation: The World Professional Association for Transgender Health (2012) suggests that physical interventions should only be undertaken following thorough exploration of psychological, family, and social issues. After this exploration, the physical interventions are approached in three categories or stages—completely reversible, partially reversible, and irreversible (surgical procedures)—beginning with the least drastic and proceeding to the next as appropriate, with continuing assessment and psychotherapy before, during, and after each stage. The completely reversible stage involves delay of puberty with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist, which suppresses testosterone or estrogen production. Other hormones can also be used to delay or stop puberty in male and female adolescents. The benefit of the puberty-suppressing regimen is that because it is fully reversible, an adolescent has some time to explore his or her gender-related issues. The partially reversible stage involves exposing the adolescent to hormones (i.e., androgens or estrogens) that will either masculinize or feminize the body; “some hormone-induced changes may need reconstructive surgery to reverse the effect (e.g., gynecomastia caused by estrogens), while other changes are not reversible (e.g., deepening of the voice caused by testosterone)” (World Professional Association for Transgender Health 2012, p. 18). Finally, the Standards of Care suggest that irreversible changes (surgical procedures) should not be carried out until an individual reaches the legal age required to give consent for medical procedures and has “lived continuously for a year” in the gender role that is congruent with his or her gender identity (World Professional Association for Transgender Health 2012).

questions.question_text: What is the beginning phase of the treatment of adult gender dysphoria?

options.text: Hormone therapy.
Bilateral orchiectomy in men and bilateral mastectomy and optional hysterectomy in women.
Encouraging the patient to live in the world in the cross-gender role.
Cognitive therapy designed to minimize the patient's dissatisfaction with his or her birth gender.
Referral to an endocrinologist and a surgeon.

correct_answer.text: Encouraging the patient to live in the world in the cross-gender role.

correct_answers.text: Encouraging the patient to live in the world in the cross-gender role.

questions.explanation: The course of treatment usually begins with the patient living in the world in the cross-gender role before surgical reassignment. The exact nature of the cross-gender role will vary from patient to patient, but males typically cross-dress, have electrolysis, and practice female behaviors, whereas women cut their hair and bind or conceal their breasts. They can even change their identity to the opposite gender on official documents and at work. After a period of time, as set by the patient and the team of professionals, and if these measures have been successful and the patient still wishes reassignment, hormone treatment can begin

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a relatively common side effect of hormone therapy during sex reassignment in men?

options.text: Kidney failure.
Depression.
Orthostatic hypotension.
Acne.
Double vision.

questions.explanation: After a period in which the patient lives in the world in the crossgender role, hormone treatment is the next step before surgical reassignment. Estrogens are given to the male patient, resulting in redistribution of body fat in a more “feminine” pattern and enlargement of the breasts. Because this treatment may have medical complications, patients should be followed up closely by a physician. Side effects of estrogen treatment may include deep vein thrombosis, thromboembolic disorders, increased blood pressure, weight gain, impaired glucose tolerance, liver abnormalities, and depression. Testosterone given to the female patient causes redistribution of fat, growth of facial and body hair, enlargement of the clitoris, and deepening of the voice. Unwanted side effects of testosterone treatment include acne, edema secondary to sodium retention, and impairment of liver function.

questions.question_text: Favorable outcomes for gender reassignment surgery have been associated with which of the following?

options.text: No preoperative psychotherapy.
Long-standing cross-dressing among family and friends.
Preoperative psychotherapy.
Postoperative psychotherapy.
Preoperative social phobia.

questions.explanation: Surgical reassignment to the opposite sex has been the most widely used and studied treatment modality for adults with gender dysphoria or gender identity disorder. Green and Fleming (1990) reviewed the literature written from 1979 through 1989 on both male-to-female and female-to-male postoperative transsexuals. Only 11 follow-up studies were located in the literature. These authors concluded that preoperative factors that were indicative of a favorable outcome included an absence of psychosis, as well as mental and emotional stability shown prior to the surgery; a successful adaptation to the desired gender for at least 1 year; an understanding of the consequences and limitations of the surgery; and the seeking of preoperative psychotherapy. Data from the report indicated that outcomes were considered satisfactory for 97% of the female-to-male transsexuals and for 87% of the male-to-female transsexuals.
